4km
beach about

north of El Nido town. A gently curving stretch of sand backed by palm forest, and the twin-beach view from the hill above are famous, making it the best place to rest for a day between island-hopping tours.
Nacpan Beach is a roughly
4km
beach in Barangay Bukana, about
17km

north of El Nido town. Unlike most of El Nido's coastline, which is made up of limestone cliffs and small pockets of sand, Nacpan is a wide, sweeping beach of soft golden sand shaped like a bow. Dense palm forest lines the beach, and the sea in front is wide open to the horizon, giving a sense of openness quite different from El Nido's island hopping.

What makes this beach special is the "twin beaches" view. Climb the small hill at the southwestern end of Nacpan Beach and you can see Nacpan and the neighboring Calitang Beach spread out on either side of a narrow sandbar. This scene, with the two beaches stretching out like wings, appears in nearly every photo introducing El Nido.

Visitors increased after the beach appeared repeatedly on foreign travel media's "best beaches in Asia" lists, but the beach is so long that you can still find a quiet spot just by walking a little further. There are only a few restaurants, bars, and glamping sites near the entrance and no large resorts, making it a good escape from the bustle of El Nido town.

It suits travelers who want to clear a day between busy island-hopping tours for swimming, napping, and beach walks, those who enjoy renting a motorbike and riding country roads, and families who want to let their kids play on a wide stretch of sand.
Climb the hill at the southwestern end of the beach for about
15–20 minutes
and you'll see both Nacpan and Calitang beaches spread out on either side. The color is best in late morning or late afternoon, when the light comes from the side.
Walk north from the beach entrance and the crowd thins until you're nearly walking alone. The soft sand is comfortable to walk barefoot.
The gently sloping sandy beach is good for swimming, and many people enjoy bodyboarding on days with waves. On high-wave days, it's safer to stay close to shore.

blocks.title: Resting in a hammock under the palms

children.text: Renting a hammock and beach chair at a beach restaurant or bar and sipping coconut juice is the best way to enjoy Nacpan.
The beach faces west, so you can watch the sky turn red at sunset. Just make sure to arrange transport in advance, since the road back to town is dark after sundown.
The road from town to Nacpan runs through rice fields, palm forest, and small villages — a beautiful drive. You can stop at a waterfall or other beaches along the way.
A small waterfall reached by walking through forest and along a stream on the way to Nacpan, usually visited with a local guide. Flow can be low near the end of the dry season.

1 hour 30 minutes–1 hour 40 minutes
from Clark. The airport is north of El Nido town, so it is actually closer to Nacpan Beach, about
20–30 minutes
by car. If you use Puerto Princesa Airport (PPS), it takes about
5–6 hours

Chartering a round-trip tricycle from El Nido town to Nacpan is the most common way. It costs about
round trip including waiting time of about
3–4 hours
, and seats up to 3–4 people, so it's cheaper with more people. Agree on the wait time and return time before you set off. The one-way ride takes about
30–40 minutes
, and the last few kilometers are unpaved or narrow, so expect a bumpy ride.
Renting a motorbike in town costs about

per day, letting you freely stop at waterfalls and other beaches. The main road is paved, but the entrance to the beach is mixed sand and gravel, so beginners should ride slowly. An international driving permit and a helmet are required.
Some travel agencies sell land tours combining Nacpan, the waterfall, and other beaches for about
per person. It's convenient and economical for a small group.
December
through
May
is the dry season and the best time to visit. In this period, the sky is clear and the sea shines a turquoise color, and viewpoint photos come out sharpest too.
March–May
has high temperatures and very strong sun, so it's best to be active in the morning or late afternoon.
Nacpan Beach is wide open to the western sea, so it's directly affected by wind and waves. From
November
to
February
, the northeast monsoon Amihan raises waves on some days, so swim with care, though it's actually good for bodysurfing.
From
June
to
October

, the southwest monsoon Habagat and the rainy season bring frequent rain, and seaweed and debris wash up on some days. The access road can turn muddy, making motorbike travel difficult, but the upside is that you can have the beach almost to yourself with fewer visitors.

Not many people stay overnight at Nacpan Beach itself, but there are a few glamping tents and bungalow-style lodgings near the entrance, letting you spend a night for about

. There's almost no artificial light at night, so the stars are vivid, and in the morning you can walk the beach with no one else around — the biggest advantage. However, power and internet are unstable and there are few amenities nearby.
Most travelers stay in El Nido town or the Lio Beach area near the airport and visit as a day trip. Town lodging runs about
per night, and resorts on the northern Lio side offer a short trip to Nacpan.
Near the beach entrance, beach restaurants and bars sell Filipino and Western food. Menus like grilled fish, shrimp dishes, chicken adobo, and fried rice cost about
per person, and coconut juice served whole and mango shakes are popular. There are almost no restaurants along the northern stretch of the beach, so bring water and snacks if you plan to walk far.
There are no ATMs near the beach, and few places take cards. Bring plenty of cash from town.
When chartering a tricycle, it's best to agree in advance on the round-trip fare, waiting time at the beach, and any extra stops such as the waterfall.
Phone signal reaches weakly only near the beach entrance and drops out almost entirely along the northern stretch. Agree on a return time with your driver beforehand.
Much of the beach has little shade, so a hat, sunglasses, and reef-safe sunscreen are essential.
The path to the twin-beach viewpoint is short but steep with slippery dirt sections, so sneakers are more comfortable than sandals.
For viewpoint photos, shoot around
10 AM
or
3–4 PM
rather than at midday, when the water color and shadows stand out more.
Always wear a helmet on a motorbike, and since there are few streetlights after dark in many stretches, it's best to head back early.
On high-wave days, strong rip currents can form off the beach. Lifeguards aren't posted along most of it, so don't venture out too far.
Coconuts can fall from the palm trees behind the beach, so it's best not to set up directly underneath them.
Sand flies and mosquitoes increase in the late afternoon, so bring insect repellent.
Motorbike accidents are fairly common. Dirt and sandy roads are especially slippery after rain, so slow down.
Take your trash back with you, and don't leave glass bottles on the beach.
